accuracy.evidence: The skill matches the UK Development Matters (2021) statement for 3- and 4-year-olds, 'Understand a question or instruction that has two parts, such as: Get your coat and wait at the door', and ASHA's age guide ('follows two-part directions, like Get the spoon and put it on the table'). The adult text's claims follow Gathercole and Alloway's working-memory guidance for teachers: children lose parts of long instructions, the last-heard part is the most likely to survive, and short instructions, repetition and saying it back help. Nothing in the lab says forgetting is naughty.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real failure patterns: doing only the last part heard (challenge tag 'last', m2 'Tom runs to lunch and leaves the ball'), doing the parts in the wrong order (tapping the door first is refused with 'Gran said the cup first', challenge tag 'swap', m1), finishing part one and drifting (cup dropped elsewhere gets 'That was part one! Part two: take it to the sink', p4, m7), and guessing instead of asking (memory-step prediction, challenge tags 'guess' and 'stop', p3, m8).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built around holding a spoken instruction in mind: a room of eight things where taps are checked against the order Gran said, a get-and-bring mode where the first tap lifts the thing and the second must be the named place (or a drag between them), a memory mode where the bubble hides after 2.4 s with a praised 'Say it again, please' button, and a first/then card order to say the steps back. No other flagship lab checks the order of spoken steps; gate_lab_distinct passes against flaglisten, flagaloud and flagplay.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each idea by doing it. Tapping the second thing first gets 'Gran said the cup first. Start with the cup'; getting the shoes and stopping shows 'Done: 1 of 2' and asks for part two; in memory mode the words vanish, so the child feels the need to hold both parts and can ask again without penalty (the step win line adds 'And you asked when you needed to'). The step text only names the rule after that ('First means do it now. Then means do it next').

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option: 'First clap, then jump' with Jump offered first (the last-heard word pulls children to it), 'Put your cup in the sink' as one part or two (it sounds like one job but is get then put), and guessing versus asking again when you forget (children often guess to avoid asking). Each is answered by the step's own tapping.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six scenario questions with two tagged wrong options each, and each tag has its own message: 'Right jobs, wrong order. Do the first part first', 'That is only the last part. Hold both parts in your head', 'One part got missed. There were two jobs', 'That was not said. If you forget, ask', and 'It is OK to forget. Ask, Can you say it again, please?'. The iPhone 13 smoke run showed the right message for every wrong answer tried.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads at FK grade -1.2 against the family target of 5.0, with lines such as 'Listen to the end. Do the first job first.' Adult text reads at 7.7 (target 10). Gran's bubble wraps onto two lines at 15 px on a 360 px screen, and the young class gives 56 px buttons with larger step text.

no_filler.evidence: gate_content finds no filler. Every kid paragraph is one move (one job, two jobs, order, asking and saying back), and the adult paragraphs give the age and why it matters, what each lab step does, the three common mistakes plus the adult habit of giving too many steps, and an everyday routine to practise. None of it is shared template text.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px Android screenshots of all six steps: the 4 x 2 grid of things gives tiles of about 80 px with 12 px names, Gran's instruction wraps inside the bubble with nothing clipped, the first/then slots and three picture cards fit side by side, and the same actions are repeated as large buttons under the canvas.

accessibility.evidence: Every action has a button with a spoken name ('Touch the ball', 'Get the shoes', then 'Take it to the door', 'Say it again, please', one button per picture card), so no drag is needed. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action (e.g. 'Good, the cup. What comes next? Gran says: First touch the cup, then the door.'), the hidden-words state is announced, and axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes on desktop and phone.
